passage:
When I got my first team at the design agency, one member, Noor, was brilliant and exhausting in the same breath. Every conflict produced a hero and a villain. In March, Arvind from finance was "the only sane person here". In April, after he questioned her invoice, he was "a snake who's always hated our team". Meanwhile Jessy, who had disagreed with her in March, was suddenly "my rock".
I'm Hafsa, and I nearly got pulled in. It's flattering when someone calls you the only fair manager. What worked was being boring. Every time Noor said someone was awful, I asked, "What exactly happened? What did they say, and when?" Usually the specific thing was small: one email, one tone. I listened, I took the real problems seriously, and I didn't agree that anyone was a saint or a snake, including me.

qa.q: What did Noor call Arvind in March?
qa.a: "The only sane person here."

qa.q: Why might sorting people into heroes and villains feel right to Noor in each conflict?
qa.a: Strong feelings in the moment make one small slight, like a question about an invoice, feel like proof of who someone really is.

qa.q: Which choice of Hafsa's kept things fair, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking what exactly happened, what was said and when, which shrank each conflict to its real size and kept Hafsa from taking sides.

qa.q: How might Arvind feel being called 'a snake' after questioning an invoice?
qa.a: Unfairly judged and wary, since he was doing his job and suddenly found himself cast as an enemy.

grounding: A manager describes a team member who sorts colleagues into saints and enemies with each conflict, and how asking for specifics kept the manager fair to everyone.

passage:
I'm Damini, and I manage the patient-support desk at a hospital in Aizawl. Lalremsiami is one of my best staff: fast, kind to patients, tireless. But over the last few months I've noticed a pattern. After every disagreement, she sorts people. When the night-shift supervisor changed the roster, he became "the enemy". When Ruth covered one of her shifts, Ruth became "the only person who has ever helped me". Two weeks later, when Ruth forgot to hand over a file, she was "useless".
I can't see inside Lalremsiami's head. Maybe she's exhausted. Maybe she's been let down a lot. So in our one-to-ones I ask for specifics: "What happened on Tuesday? What did Ruth actually say?" Then I check with the others, and I treat everyone the same, whoever is the hero this week.

qa.q: What did Ruth forget to hand over?
qa.a: A file.

qa.q: Why might Lalremsiami switch so quickly from 'the only person who has ever helped me' to 'useless'?
qa.a: Damini guesses she may be exhausted or often let down, so each small letdown feels total and wipes out the earlier help.

qa.q: Which of Damini's choices keep things fair, and why?
qa.a: Asking for specifics in one-to-ones and checking with others, so decisions rest on what happened rather than on who is hero or villain this week.

qa.q: How might Ruth feel going from 'the only person who has ever helped me' to 'useless'?
qa.a: Confused and hurt, since she was the same colleague both times and only forgot one file.

grounding: A manager notices a staff member sorting colleagues into heroes and enemies after each conflict, asks for specifics and stays fair to all.

passage:
Monday. In the stand-up, Mohit told Sudha that the new tester, Aarti, was "a lifesaver, the best hire this year". Sudha nodded and noted the bug Aarti had found.
Thursday. After Aarti flagged three of Mohit's features as broken, Mohit came to Sudha's desk. "She's out to get me. She's sabotaging the release." Sudha said, "Which three bugs? Let's look at them together." They went through each one. Two were real. One was a misunderstanding in the ticket.
The next Tuesday. Mohit started calling the design lead "a genius" for backing his idea. Sudha smiled. "Glad it helped. What specifically did he change?"
Mohit paused, then laughed a little. "You always make me get specific."
"I do," Sudha said, and pulled up the design notes.

qa.q: How many of Aarti's flagged bugs turned out to be real?
qa.a: Two were real; one was a misunderstanding in the ticket.

qa.q: Why did Mohit suddenly feel Aarti was 'out to get me'?
qa.a: Having his features flagged stung, and in that moment it felt like an attack, wiping out his earlier view of her as a lifesaver.

qa.q: What choice did Sudha make on Thursday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Going through the three bugs with Mohit one by one, which turned a story about sabotage into specific facts that could be fixed.

qa.q: How might Aarti feel if she heard she was 'sabotaging the release'?
qa.a: Hurt and unfairly accused, since she was doing her job by flagging bugs, two of which were real.

grounding: Over a week a manager notices a developer casting colleagues as heroes or villains with each conflict, and keeps asking for specifics to stay fair.

passage:
"Kunal, you say your new analyst calls one colleague a genius and the next a traitor, week by week? Sit. Your Bhavna ma'am had one of those too.
I was twenty-five, managing the front desk of a hotel in Shimla. Vimal was quick and charming. In June the housekeeping head was 'the only person who actually works here'. In July, after she questioned one of his bookings, she was 'a snake, out to get me'. By August the new trainee was the saint, and I was, I heard, 'useless'.
I didn't take sides. Each time he brought me a hero or a villain, I asked the same thing: 'What exactly happened? What was said, and when?' Usually the answer was one small event. I wrote down the facts, dealt with those, and treated everyone the same in meetings.
It didn't change Vimal overnight. But the team stopped splitting in two."

qa.q: Who was "the only person who actually works here" in June?
qa.a: The housekeeping head.

qa.q: Why might Vimal's labels have felt true to him each time?
qa.a: Each small conflict brought strong feelings, and in that moment people seemed wholly good or wholly against him, so the labels felt like accurate descriptions.

qa.q: What question did Bhavna ask, and why did it help?
qa.a: "What exactly happened? What was said, and when?" It shrank the saints and villains down to single events she could handle fairly.

qa.q: How might the housekeeping head have felt going from praised to "a snake"?
qa.a: She would likely feel confused and wary, since one question about a booking suddenly turned praise into hostility.

grounding: Shows, through a senior manager's memory, a manager who notices a staff member sorting colleagues into saints and enemies and responds by asking for specifics and staying fair.

passage:
It was the week before Diwali, the warehouse in Guwahati was running double shifts, and half the loading team was out with flu. Siddharth, twenty-five and three months into his first manager job, had forty trucks to dispatch by Friday.
Pradeep caught him by the loading bay. "Sir, Moni is useless. She's sabotaging my shift. Everyone knows it." Last month Moni had been "the only one here I trust". And yesterday's villain, Ravi from inventory, was apparently a hero today.
Siddharth had no time for this. It would have been easy to nod and move Moni off the shift. Instead he opened the notes on his phone. "Okay. What exactly happened, and when?"
Pradeep paused. "Yesterday. The truck left twenty minutes late."
"Because?"
"...The pallets weren't wrapped. That was my part, actually. She was waiting on me."
Siddharth wrote it down, kept Moni on the shift, and asked both of them to meet him after the rush.

qa.q: How late did the truck leave?
qa.a: Twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been thinking when it would have been easy to nod along?
qa.a: Siddharth was probably stressed and tempted to take Pradeep's word with forty trucks and staff out sick, but he seemed to sense that fairness needed the facts first.

qa.q: What did asking for specifics reveal, and why did it matter?
qa.a: It showed the delay came from Pradeep's own unwrapped pallets, not Moni, so Siddharth could keep Moni on the shift and stay fair to everyone.

qa.q: What would change for Moni if Siddharth had simply moved her off the shift?
qa.a: Moni would have been punished for someone else's delay and branded a villain, likely feeling bewildered and losing trust in her manager.

grounding: Illustrates a new manager under festival-rush pressure who notices a team member casting colleagues as heroes and villains and asks for the specific facts before acting.
